title: The middle sky and the hand trick
teaches: Altocumulus and altostratus, and how to judge a cloud’s height using your hand and its shadows

blocks.text: Look up past the hilltops. The middle floor is the hardest to read from the ground, but it is the most useful for forecasting once you know what to look for.

The middle floor runs from about two to seven kilometres up, where the air is near or below freezing and clouds usually consist of a mixture of liquid droplets and ice crystals. On most days, thermals rising from the sun-warmed ground never reach this high; the atmosphere above a kilometre or two is stable, so rising bubbles lose their buoyancy on the low floor where fair-weather cumulus clouds flatten out. (On days with deep instability, storm towers punch through every floor, which we will examine in the final lesson.)

Middle-floor clouds usually form a different way: by broad, gentle lifting, as a wide layer of moist air glides slowly upward over hundreds of kilometres. This happens most often out in front of a storm. That word needs some care here, because it is used for two very different things.

The storm most people picture is a **thunderstorm**: a single towering cloud (cumulonimbus) a few kilometres across, built by warm air bubbling straight up from the ground, usually on a hot afternoon. It grows in an hour, pours for less than an hour and drifts on. A thunderstorm is a heap cloud from the second lesson grown enormous, and it gets the final lesson to itself.

The other kind is a **frontal storm**, the kind behind a long grey day of steady rain or snow. It is not one cloud but a whole weather system, often a thousand kilometres across, that takes a day or two to pass over. At its heart, a mass of warm, moist air runs into a mass of colder air. Cold air is denser, so it stays low and hugs the ground as a long, thin wedge, and the warm air does not push it aside but slides up over the top of it. The line on the ground where the two meet is called a **front**.

The top of that wedge slopes very gently, rising about one kilometre for every hundred to two hundred kilometres along the ground. So the warm air gliding up it reaches the middle and high floors far ahead of the front itself. From the cold side, you see the storm’s cloud long before its rain: first thin, high cirrus, then middle-floor sheets a few hundred kilometres out, and finally thick, low rain cloud (nimbostratus) as the front draws near. That is why middle-floor clouds arrive well *ahead* of a storm, often by half a day or more. And just as on the low floor, lifting a wide layer all together produces flat sheets. Reading a front as it comes, hour by hour, is the subject of the seventh lesson.

blocks.caption: A frontal storm seen side-on: warm air gliding up over a wedge of cold air.

blocks.text: A cloud sheet on the middle floor does not always stay smooth, however. Just as the ground cools at night by radiating infrared light out to space, clouds radiate infrared energy too. The top of a cloud layer radiates infrared heat straight up into the cold, clear sky above and receives very little radiation back, so the top of the cloud cools steadily. Meanwhile, the base of the cloud faces the warmer ground below, absorbing roughly as much infrared heat from the earth as it radiates downward. During the day, sunlight warms the cloud top slightly, but because white cloud droplets reflect most incoming sunlight, infrared cooling still dominates for most of the day and night. As a result, the top of the cloud layer grows progressively colder than its base.

Inside a cloud, a parcel of air moving up or down changes temperature by only about 5 °C per kilometre, because condensing or evaporating water droplets release or absorb latent heat (the stored heat from the second lesson). Once radiative cooling makes the top of the cloud layer more than 5 °C per kilometre colder than the base, the layer becomes unstable within itself. A pocket of chilled, dense air at the top sinks and stays colder than the cloudy air around it, while warmer air from the base rises to take its place. The layer begins to overturn in regular convection cells, each forming a loop with rising air in one place and sinking air right beside it.

Loops that are much wider than they are tall have to drag air a long way horizontally, while loops that are very narrow experience too much friction against their neighbours, so the cells naturally settle into roughly equal width and height, about as wide as the cloud layer is deep (typically a few hundred metres). Where air rises in each cell, the cloud thickens into a rounded lump; where air sinks, the droplets evaporate and the cloud thins or clears. In this way, a smooth cloud sheet breaks up into a pattern of rounded patches or rolls. (The same cooling at the cloud top also helps keep stratocumulus decks on the low floor stirred and broken into lumps, along with the heating from below.)

blocks.caption: A cloud layer cooled from the top, turning over in cells.

blocks.text: The middle floor therefore displays the same two basic textures as the low floor, named with the prefix *alto-*. **Altostratus** is the smooth, unbroken sheet, while **altocumulus** is the layer of rounded patches or rolls separated by lanes of clear sky, often compared to a flock of sheep.

At first glance, a layer of altocumulus looks very similar to **stratocumulus** on the low floor or **cirrocumulus** on the high floor. All three consist of patches or rolls arranged in a layer, and from the ground there are no landmarks in the sky to judge their altitude against. How can you tell which floor the layer is on?

You can judge their height by the apparent size of the individual cloud elements. Because overturning cells are roughly as wide as their cloud layer is deep, low and middle cloud layers (both typically a few hundred metres thick) break into lumps that are a few hundred metres across. High-floor cloud layers are much shallower, often less than a hundred metres thick, so cirrocumulus ripples are physically smaller as well as much further away. Just as a car looks smaller in the distance, the higher a cloud layer sits, the smaller its individual lumps *look* from the ground.

In the figure, which views the sky high up where you would normally measure, a 300-metre lump at an altitude of 2 km spans an **angle** of about 7° across your field of view; at 5 km up it spans about 3°, and a 100-metre grain at 9 km spans less than 1°.

You always carry a reliable ruler for measuring angles: your own hand held at arm’s length. With your arm stretched out straight, a closed fist covers about 10° of sky, three fingers side by side cover about 5°, a thumb covers about 2°, and the nail of your little finger covers about 1°. Because people with larger hands also have proportionally longer arms that hold the hand further from the eye, the geometry cancels out and these angles hold true for almost everyone.

blocks.caption: A layer of lumpy cloud, seen from the ground with your arm stretched out.
blocks.task: Move the layer through the three floors and see each verdict.

blocks.text: This gives a practical rule of thumb with your arm fully extended: cloud elements **wider than three fingers** are stratocumulus, elements between a **little-finger nail and three fingers** (roughly the width of a thumb) are altocumulus, and elements **smaller than your little-finger nail** are cirrocumulus. Always measure clouds high up in the sky, well away from the horizon. Near the horizon, you are looking at clouds that are much further away and viewing them obliquely from the side, which makes every element appear foreshortened and deceptively small.

Shading provides a second clue to a cloud’s floor. When sunlight enters the top of a cloud, the water droplets scatter the light in all directions, bouncing much of it right back out the top. The deeper light travels into the cloud, the less of it remains to emerge from the bottom. A very thin cloud lets most of the sunlight pass through and looks uniformly white from underneath. A cloud lump several hundred metres thick, on the other hand, reflects most of the sunlight back into space and lets much less reach its base, so from the ground you see a shaded underside: grey in the centre with bright white edges where sunlight catches the thinner sides. (The base looks grey rather than pitch black because some diffused sunlight still filters through from above, while the ground and surrounding sky reflect light upward from below.)

blocks.caption: One lump of cloud with the sun above it.
blocks.task: Thicken the cloud until it shades itself.

blocks.text: Altocumulus elements are usually deep enough to show **shaded bellies**, looking like grey-bottomed sheep in a flock. Cirrocumulus, being thin and composed of ice crystals high aloft, consists of pure white grains with **no shading at all**. Checking for shading quickly distinguishes altocumulus from cirrocumulus, while the hand test distinguishes altocumulus from lower, larger stratocumulus.

There is one special variety of altocumulus always worth watching for. If you spot miniature turrets sprouting upward from a line of altocumulus on a warm, humid morning, that is altocumulus castellanus, from the Latin for castle-like. Those little towers tell you that the middle sky is cooling with height faster than the 5 °C per kilometre of a rising cloudy parcel, so parcels rising out of the cloud layer stay warmer than their surroundings and keep climbing on their own. On a normal day, the afternoon thermals are capped well below the middle floor; when castellanus appears in the morning, it warns that the middle floor is already unstable and afternoon thermals can punch all the way up into thunderstorms.

**Altostratus** is the smooth, featureless sheet of the middle floor, forming a grey or bluish-grey layer of mixed water droplets and ice crystals that often covers the entire sky. It is too thick for you to see the sharp outline of the sun, yet thin enough in places for the sun to shine through faintly as a pale disc, as if viewed through frosted glass.

blocks.caption: The sun behind thin, thicker and very thick cloud.

blocks.text: Two simple checks distinguish altostratus from thinner or thicker sheets. First, under altostratus, **shadows vanish**. Because the cloud deck scatters sunlight thoroughly, most of the light reaching the ground comes evenly from the entire overcast sky rather than in a direct beam from the sun, illuminating objects from all sides and filling in shadows.

Second, altostratus produces **no halo** around the sun. An optical halo forms when ice crystals bend sunlight by a fixed angle (22°), which only stays visible in a thin ice veil where a ray of sunlight passes through a single crystal on its way to your eye. In a deep altostratus deck containing both droplets and ice, each light ray is scattered repeatedly from particle to particle in new directions, scrambling any 22° ring into an even glow. (We will examine halos and high ice veils in the next lesson, along with the thicker rain layer shown at the end of the slider.)
Altostratus rarely sits still for long. Most often it arrives as a thickening, lowering veil ahead of an approaching storm system, warning that steady rain is on the way.

For each photo, decide which floor the cloud belongs to: low, middle, or high. For cumulus heaps, report the floor where the base sits. On lumpy layers, use the hand test and check for shaded bellies; on smooth sheets or wispy streaks, use what you know about their edges and how the sun shines through.

The sky over a few hours. What is it up to?

items.question: Patches of altocumulus at breakfast have merged into a grey sheet. By early afternoon the sun is a pale disc, as if behind frosted glass, and shadows have gone. What is the sky up to?
options: A storm system is coming: expect the cloud to lower and steady rain later
Fair weather: the sheet will burn off by evening
items.why: A middle-floor sheet that keeps thickening is the broad, gentle lifting far out ahead of an approaching front. Altostratus thick enough to wipe out shadows usually lowers into steady rain within hours.

items.question: High overhead is a layer of rounded lumps with grey bellies. At arm’s length, each lump is about as wide as your thumb. Which floor is it on?
items.why: Measured high in the sky, lumps between a little-finger nail and three fingers wide are altocumulus. The shaded bellies rule out the thin, pure white grains of cirrocumulus.

learned: Middle-floor clouds usually form from broad, gentle lifting, as when warm air glides up over a wedge of cold air ahead of a frontal storm (not a thunderstorm); when the top of a cloud layer cools by radiating infrared heat to space, the layer overturns into cellular lumps.
Held at arm’s length, a closed fist spans about 10° of sky, three fingers 5°, a thumb 2°, and a little-finger nail 1°.
High in the sky, cloud lumps wider than three fingers are stratocumulus, those between a little-finger nail and three fingers are altocumulus, and grains smaller than a nail are cirrocumulus.
Deeper cloud lumps shade their own bases: altocumulus elements have grey undersides, whereas thin cirrocumulus grains are bright white with no shading.
Altostratus shows the sun dimly as if through frosted glass, casting no ground shadows and forming no halo; it usually thickens ahead of steady rain.
Small turrets sprouting from altocumulus (castellanus) show that the middle atmosphere is unstable, warning of possible afternoon thunderstorms.

hand-trick.title: The hand trick
hand-trick.text: With your arm stretched out straight, a closed fist covers about 10° of sky, three fingers 5°, a thumb 2°, and a little-finger nail 1°. Because higher cloud layers are further away, their individual lumps look smaller: elements wider than three fingers are stratocumulus, elements between a nail and three fingers are altocumulus, and grains smaller than a nail are cirrocumulus. Grey, shaded undersides indicate a thicker layer of droplets (stratocumulus or altocumulus, never cirrocumulus).

altocumulus.title: Altocumulus
altocumulus.text: Rounded patches or rolls with grey, shaded bellies on the middle floor, spanning between a little-finger nail and three fingers at arm’s length. They form when a middle-level cloud sheet cools at its top by radiating infrared energy and overturns into convection cells. Morning turrets (castellanus) indicate middle-level instability and warn of afternoon thunderstorms.

altostratus.title: Altostratus
altostratus.text: A uniform grey or bluish sheet of mixed droplets and ice crystals on the middle floor. The sun shines through dimly as if behind frosted glass, casting no shadows on the ground and producing no optical halo. It typically arrives as a thickening veil ahead of steady rain, with precipitation likely within a few hours.
